title: Thin places
hook: places where heaven and earth feel close

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessings for everything. Your line was bless the fire. Did the stove or the kettle get its breath? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

A man on the run sleeps outdoors with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and angels going up and down on it. That's Jacob, in Genesis, fleeing his brother. When he wakes, he says, in the King James words: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." A bare patch of hillside had turned out to be a doorway. People who pray in the Celtic way have a name for spots like that. Today: thin places.

A thin place, as people use the phrase, is somewhere the distance between heaven and earth seems to shrink, where the veil feels thin. Some name Iona, the small island off the west of Scotland linked with Saint Columba. Others name a mountain, a shoreline, a ruined chapel, a back pew. This lesson won't claim an ancient source for the phrase itself. What's old is the experience. Jacob's words go on: "How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Dreadful, in the old sense: full of awe. The gate of heaven, in a place with no temple, no altar, nothing but a stone. And Jacob does something with that stone. He sets it up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. Here's a tension Christians hold. Psalm one hundred thirty-nine, the psalm of the circle two days ago, asks where anyone could go to get away from God's presence, and its answer is nowhere. So why would some places feel thinner than others? One way Christians put it: it isn't that God is closer there. It's that people are more awake there. Some places strip away the noise: wind, water, height, old stones, or simply a room where something true once happened. Jacob's own line holds both halves. The Lord was in this place, and I knew it not. The thinness was on his side. That's why a thin place doesn't have to be famous. A kitchen where someone you loved used to cook. A bench where someone heard hard news and somehow got through it. A small chapel in the middle of the night.
screen: `THE GATE OF HEAVEN, AT A STONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit or remember a thin place. If there's one near you, a window, a tree, a corner of a church, go there now or soon. If not, remember one: somewhere that, for whatever reason, seemed close to something more. See it clearly. The light, the sounds, where you stood. Don't explain it. Just go back to it for a while. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words: surely the LORD is in this place. The bell holds the time.
Thin places. Places where heaven and earth feel close, like Jacob's stone at Bethel: the gate of heaven, found on bare ground.
Your line: heaven is thin here. Today, in one ordinary spot, stop and say it under your breath, and see whether you'd been missing something. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Some Christians make pilgrimages to places such as Iona, or keep a small local place, a chapel, a shore or a garden, where they go to pray; the idea of thin places is used in Celtic-style spirituality and retreat work.

notes: The script deliberately makes no claim about the age or origin of the phrase 'thin place'; it is often presented as ancient Celtic but its documented use may be recent. Confirm the framing.
Iona is described only as 'linked with Saint Columba'; confirm.
'Dreadful, in the old sense: full of awe' glosses the KJV word; confirm.
'One way Christians put it: it isn't that God is closer there; people are more awake there' is presented as one view, not the tradition's single teaching. Confirm.
Original: בֵּית־אֵל (Beit El). Confirm pointing and pronunciation; the note avoids a direct etymology claim, but the name is commonly glossed 'house of God'.
Psalm 139:7–10 paraphrased (no escape from God's presence); Psalm 139:5 was quoted on day 1149.
